concepts.label: I/O devices and the storage hierarchy

steps.question: Your processor can run billions of instructions per second. Why does opening a big file still make you wait?
clues: A disk access takes **millions of CPU cycles**.
**Random** accesses are far slower than **sequential** ones.
Overall speed is limited by the slowest part: **I/O**.

notes.explain: Let students guess before revealing the clues.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: Inside a hard disk drive (HDD)

items: **Platters**: spinning magnetic disks (for example 7,200 revolutions per minute)
**Tracks** are concentric circles; each is divided into **sectors** (typically 512 bytes or 4 KiB)
A **head** on a moving arm reads and writes; all heads move together
A request needs the arm to move to the right track, then wait for the sector to rotate under the head

steps.why: Because a disk has mechanical parts, its access time is measured in milliseconds, a million times slower than a register.
steps.real: Hard disks still store most of the world's data because they are cheap per byte.

explainAgain.beginner: A record player: the needle (head) must move to the right groove (track) and then wait for the song (sector) to come around.

steps.title: The four parts of a disk access

head: Part
What it is
Typical
rows: Moving the arm to the right track
3 to 10 ms (average about 4 ms is common)
Waiting for the sector to arrive under the head; on average half a rotation
Reading the data as it passes under the head
The disk controller and the bus

terms.t: access time = seek + rotational latency + transfer + overhead
terms.note: the sum of the four parts

steps.why: Seek and rotation dominate: the transfer is tiny. That is why disks love big, sequential transfers.
steps.real: Faster spindles (10,000 or 15,000 RPM) cut the rotational latency to 3 or 2 ms.

mistake.wrong: Rotational latency is a full rotation.
mistake.right: On average the sector is half a rotation away.

steps.title: Calculate: disk access time

blocks.title: Average disk access time (illustrative numbers)
blocks.equation: Access time = seek + rotational latency + transfer + controller overhead

steps.why: A random 4 KB read takes 8.31 ms: about 120 requests per second, or only 0.49 MB/s on a drive that can stream 100 MB/s. Raise the request size to 1024 KB and watch the throughput climb.

steps.question: A 7,200 RPM disk. What is the average rotational latency?

reveal.text: One rotation takes 60 ÷ 7,200 s = 8.33 ms. On average the data is half a rotation away: **4.17 ms**.

steps.question: Average seek 4 ms, 7,200 RPM, 100 MB/s, controller overhead 0.1 ms. How long does a 4 KB random read take?

reveal.text: 4 + 4.17 + 0.04 + 0.1 = **8.31 ms**. The 4 KB transfer is only 0.04 ms: almost all the time is mechanical.

steps.result: Reading 4 KB from DRAM takes tens of nanoseconds: a million times faster.

steps.title: Flash memory and SSDs

items: **Flash** stores data as trapped charge in transistors; it keeps its data without power (non-volatile)
An **SSD** (solid-state drive) is many flash chips plus a controller: no moving parts
Reads are by **page** (a few KB); there is no seek time or rotational latency
Random reads take tens to hundreds of microseconds, about **100 times faster than a disk**

steps.why: Flash fills the gap between DRAM and disks: much faster than a disk, much larger than DRAM.
steps.real: Phones, tablets and most laptops use flash as their main storage.

explainAgain.beginner: A bookshelf with every book instantly reachable, versus a library where a robot arm must fetch each one.

steps.title: How flash differs from RAM

items: A flash page cannot be overwritten in place: its **block** must be **erased** first
Erasing is slow and wears the cells out (thousands of cycles)
The controller hides this with a **flash translation layer** (remapping and **wear levelling**)
Writes are therefore more complicated than reads, and writing many small random updates can be slower than reading

steps.why: Flash is fast but has a very different write behaviour from RAM, and the controller does a lot of work to hide it.
steps.real: SSD lifetimes are quoted in terabytes written because the cells wear out.

mistake.wrong: An SSD can be rewritten forever like RAM.
mistake.right: Each block survives a limited number of erase cycles.

steps.statement: Flash memory keeps its data when the power is off.
steps.why: It is non-volatile, unlike DRAM and SRAM.

steps.prompt: One statement about flash is wrong. Click it.

steps.explain: Each block survives only a limited number of erase cycles (wear).

steps.title: Sequential vs random access

head: Access pattern
What happens on a disk
Result
rows: One seek and one rotational wait, then data streams under the head
near the full transfer rate (about 100 MB/s)
A seek and a rotational wait for every request

steps.why: The same data takes 200 times longer if it is scattered, so software and file systems work hard to keep data contiguous.
steps.real: Defragmenting a disk, database indexes and log-structured file systems all exist to turn random access into sequential access.

mistake.wrong: Disk speed is a single number (MB/s).
mistake.right: The speed depends enormously on whether the accesses are sequential or random.

steps.question: Reading 10 MB as 2,441 random 4 KB blocks on the disk above takes about 20 seconds. How long does a sequential read take at 100 MB/s?

reveal.text: 10 MB ÷ 100 MB/s = **0.1 s**: about 200 times faster than the random reads.

steps.result: The data transferred is identical; only the access pattern changed.

steps.title: Latency, bandwidth and IOPS

head: Measure
Meaning
Unit
rows: Time for one request from issue to completion
I/O operations per second (small random requests)

terms.t: IOPS = 1 ÷ latency (one request at a time)

steps.why: Different applications need different measures: a video stream needs bandwidth, a database needs low latency and many IOPS.
steps.real: Datasheets give sequential MB/s and random IOPS separately for this reason.

deeper.text: Several outstanding requests can overlap their latencies, which is how SSDs reach hundreds of thousands of IOPS.

steps.title: I/O limits the speed-up (Amdahl again)

blocks.title: Amdahl's Law with I/O
blocks.equation: Speedup = 1 ÷ (I/O fraction + (1 − I/O fraction) ÷ CPU speed-up)

inputs.label: Share of time spent on I/O

steps.why: If 10% of the time is I/O, a CPU that is 10 times faster speeds the whole program up only 5.26 times, and even an infinitely fast CPU can reach at most 10 times.

steps.question: A program spends 10% of its time on I/O. The CPU becomes 10 times faster; the disk does not change. What is the overall speed-up?

reveal.text: Speed-up = 1 ÷ (0.1 + 0.9 ÷ 10) = 1 ÷ 0.19 = **5.26**. The unchanged I/O part limits the gain.

steps.result: With a 100 times faster CPU it is only 9.17.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: A company doubles its servers' CPU speed but the web pages do not load noticeably faster. What could be the cause?
steps.answer: The time may be dominated by I/O (disk or network), which the faster CPU does not change. By Amdahl's Law the overall speed-up is limited by the fraction of time that does not improve; the fix is to speed up the storage (flash, caching) or the network.

questions.q: Name the four parts of a disk access.
questions.a: Seek, rotational latency, transfer time and controller overhead.

questions.q: Why is random access slow on a disk?
questions.a: Every request pays a seek and a rotational wait.

questions.q: What does Amdahl's Law say about I/O?
questions.a: I/O time that does not speed up limits the overall gain.

sections.label: I/O devices and the storage hierarchy

steps.title: I/O devices

items: The CPU talks to devices through registers at special addresses (memory-mapped I/O)
**Polling**: the CPU repeatedly asks the device if it is ready (wastes time)
**Interrupts**: the device signals the CPU when it needs attention
**DMA** (direct memory access): a controller moves whole blocks between device and memory without the CPU

steps.why: The range of speeds is enormous, so the system uses buffering, interrupts and DMA to keep the fast CPU from waiting on slow devices.
steps.real: When you copy a file the CPU only starts the transfer; the DMA engine and the disk do the rest.

steps.title: The storage hierarchy

blocks.text: Storage extends the memory hierarchy of Class 17 downward: each level is bigger and slower.

steps.why: Capacity and cost per byte improve as latency gets worse, exactly like the cache levels.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a disk read using DMA and an interrupt in order.
items: The CPU programs the DMA controller and the disk with the request
The disk seeks and reads the sector

steps.why: The CPU is free during the middle three steps.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: Where would you use flash, a hard disk and a cloud archive in a photo-sharing service?
ideas: Flash for the database and recently uploaded photos (fast random access).
Hard disks for the large store of older photos.
A cloud archive for backups and photos nobody has opened in years.
The hierarchy balances cost against access time.

steps.title: Exam practice: Amdahl

steps.question: Explain why random access is so slow on a hard disk but not on an SSD.
steps.answer: A hard disk must move the head to the right track (seek) and wait for the sector to rotate under it for every random request, which costs milliseconds, while the transfer itself takes microseconds. An SSD has no moving parts, so any page can be read after a short electronic delay of tens to hundreds of microseconds.
steps.solution: A strong answer names seek and rotation as the cause.
steps.mistake: Saying SSDs have faster transfer rates only.
steps.title: Exam practice: conceptual
What you should remember
remember: A disk access = seek + rotational latency (half a rotation on average) + transfer + controller overhead.
Seek and rotation dominate, so random access is about 200 times slower than sequential.
Flash has no mechanical delay; blocks must be erased before rewriting, and cells wear out.
Latency is time per request; bandwidth is bytes per second; throughput = IOPS × request size.
Amdahl's Law: unchanged I/O time limits overall speed-up.
DMA and interrupts keep the CPU from waiting on slow devices; the storage hierarchy trades speed for capacity.

mistakes.right: It depends on sequential vs random access.

mistakes.wrong: Rotational latency is a full rotation.
A faster CPU always speeds everything up.
mistakes.right: I/O time does not change; Amdahl's Law limits the gain.
A block must be erased before pages can be rewritten.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: Disks pay a seek and a rotational delay per request, so random access is about 200 times slower than sequential. Flash has no mechanical delay but wears out and must erase blocks before rewriting. I/O is described by latency, bandwidth and IOPS, and by Amdahl's Law the unimproved I/O time limits the overall speed-up. DMA, interrupts and a storage hierarchy hide these delays.
